1.q: וְ֠⁠נַעֲמָן שַׂר־צְבָ֨א מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֜ם הָיָ֣ה אִישׁ֩ גָּד֨וֹל לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י אֲדֹנָי⁠ו֙ וּ⁠נְשֻׂ֣א פָנִ֔ים כִּֽי־ב֛⁠וֹ נָֽתַן־יְהוָ֥ה תְּשׁוּעָ֖ה לַ⁠אֲרָ֑ם
1.note: The author is introducing **Naaman** as a new participant in the story. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation.

1.q: וְ֠⁠נַעֲמָן שַׂר־צְבָ֨א מֶֽלֶךְ־אֲרָ֜ם הָיָ֣ה אִישׁ֩ גָּד֨וֹל לִ⁠פְנֵ֤י אֲדֹנָי⁠ו֙ וּ⁠נְשֻׂ֣א פָנִ֔ים כִּֽי־ב֛⁠וֹ נָֽתַן־יְהוָ֥ה תְּשׁוּעָ֖ה לַ⁠אֲרָ֑ם
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Now since Yahweh gave deliverance to Aram through Naaman, the commander of the army of the king of Aram, he was a great man to the face of his master, and he was lifted of face]

In this context, the phrase **to the face of** means “in front of,” as in 4:12 and similar instances. But here it conveys the further idea that Naaman was where the king of Aram could see him, and so it indicates the regard that the king had for him. Alternate translation: [in the regard of his master]

The expression **was lifted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and his master lifted his face]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [and his master respected him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deliverance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh delivered Aram from its enemies]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And he was a valiant man]

The author intends for readers to understand a contrast between the facts that Naaman was **might of valor** and that he was **a leper**. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but he was a leper]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:6. Alternate translation: [Aramean soldiers]

In this context, the phrase **to the face of** means that this **girl** was “in front of” the **wife of Naaman**, but it conveys the further idea that she was there because she was her servant. Alternate translation: [And she was a servant of the wife of Naaman]

3.note: The servant girl is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, a wish. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the girl was wishing for. Alternate translation: [I wish that]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [was in the presence of] or [could go and see]

The servant girl is using the expression **remove him from his leprosy** to mean “cure him of his leprosy” or “heal his leprosy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verses 6 and 7. Alternate translation: [Then he would remove his leprosy from him]

4.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Naaman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Naaman came]

4.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר כָּ⁠זֹ֤את וְ⁠כָ⁠זֹאת֙ דִּבְּרָ֣ה הַֽ⁠נַּעֲרָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר מֵ⁠אֶ֥רֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
4.note: Naaman did not actually say the words **Like this and like this**. The author is using that expression to summarize what Naaman told the king of Aram. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see what you decided to do in the case of the same expression in 1 Kings 14:5. Alternate translation: [telling him what the girl who was from the land of Israel had said]

5.note: The king of Aram is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. (The brevity of this statement may indicate immediate agreement and urgency, and you may wish to show that in your translation.) Alternate translation: [All right, go from here in Aram right away and enter the land of Israel]

The author does not mean that Naaman somehow held all of this **silver** and **gold** and clothing in his **hand**. He is using the term “hand” to indicate that Naaman was the agent who conveyed these things, probably commanding soldiers who carried them. (The author says in 5:9 that he came with horses and chariots, and the author refers in 5:15 to his “camp,” meaning his soldiers.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 8:10. Alternate translation: [and he had his servants convey]

These 10 **kikkars of silver** weighed over 330 kilograms or about 750 pounds. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “kikkar” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and 6,000 gold shekels]

These 6,000 shekels of **gold** would have weighed nearly 70 kilograms or about 150 pounds. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “shekel” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

6.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation, but it is a quotation of what the king of Aram wrote in the letter, not something that Naaman said to the king of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the letter said]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce an important point. Sometimes, as in this case, they would use it at the beginning of a letter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. See how you translated this expression in 3:23.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.

7.q: הַ⁠אֱלֹהִ֥ים אָ֨נִי֙ לְ⁠הָמִ֣ית וּֽ⁠לְ⁠הַחֲי֔וֹת כִּֽי־זֶה֙ שֹׁלֵ֣חַ אֵלַ֔⁠י לֶ⁠אֱסֹ֥ף אִ֖ישׁ מִ⁠צָּֽרַעְתּ֑⁠וֹ
7.note: The king of Israel is using the question form to emphasize that he cannot heal Naaman. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am not God, killing and making alive, so this man should not be sending to me to remove a man from his leprosy!]
Here the word **For**, together with the word **surely**, introduces what the king believes is an obvious inference. Alternate translation: [Since that is obviously not the case,]

The king of Israel is using **know and see** as a common expression of his culture to mean “consider carefully.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 20:7. Alternate translation: [consider carefully]

The implied “you” in the imperatives **know** and **see** is plural because the king is addressing his court officials. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

8.note: Elisha is using the question form to suggest to the king of Israel that he did not need to respond so dramatically to the Aramean king’s letter. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You did not need to tear your clothes!]

10.note: Elisha is speaking of Naaman’s **flesh** as if it were a living thing that could return to him on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and your flesh will be restored to its former condition]

While the expression **be clean** is an imperative, this was not a command that Naaman was capable of obeying. Instead, it describes what the result would be if Naaman did obey Elisha’s instructions to **wash** in the **Jordan** River **seven times**. Alternate translation: [and you will become clean] or [and you will no longer be a leper]

11.q: אָמַ֜רְתִּי אֵלַ֣⁠י ׀ יֵצֵ֣א יָצ֗וֹא וְ⁠עָמַד֙ וְ⁠קָרָא֙ בְּ⁠שֵׁם־יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠הֵנִ֥יף יָד֛⁠וֹ אֶל־הַ⁠מָּק֖וֹם וְ⁠אָסַ֥ף הַ⁠מְּצֹרָֽע
11.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I said to myself that coming out, he would come out, and he would stand, and he would call on the name of Yahweh his God, and he would wave his hand over the place, and he would remove the leprosy]

Naaman is repeating forms of the verb **come out** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [He will certainly come out]

Naaman is using **call on the name of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “pray to by name.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Kings 18:24. Alternate translation: [and he will call on Yahweh his God by name] or [and he will specifically invoke Yahweh his God]

12.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֡א טוֹב֩ אבנה וּ⁠פַרְפַּ֜ר נַהֲר֣וֹת דַּמֶּ֗שֶׂק מִ⁠כֹּל֙ מֵימֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הֲ⁠לֹֽא־אֶרְחַ֥ץ בָּ⁠הֶ֖ם וְ⁠טָהָ֑רְתִּי
12.note: Naaman is using the question form to express his indignation. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statement or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [Certainly Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, are better than all of the waters of Israel! If I want to become clean, I should bathe in them!]
The author is speaking as if Naaman’s anger were actually **heat**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in a rage]

13.note: While the author says that Naaman’s **servants** approached him, it is clear that one servant is speaking on behalf of all of them, since he uses the singular pronoun **My**. It may be more natural in some languages to use a plural pronoun, since the servant is speaking for a group. Alternate translation: [Our father]
This servant is referring to Naaman by a respectful title. Use a comparable title or expression for addressing someone respectfully in your language. Alternate translation: [Master]

13.q: אָבִי֙ דָּבָ֣ר גָּד֗וֹל הַ⁠נָּבִ֛יא דִּבֶּ֥ר אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא תַעֲשֶׂ֑ה
13.note: Naaman’s servants are using the question form to try to convince him to obey Elisha. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [if the prophet spoke a great matter to you, you would certainly do it!]

The servants are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Then how much more should you do it]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [he has told you to wash and be clean]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:10. Alternate translation: [Wash, and you will become clean!]

14.note: See how you translated the comparable expression “go up” in 1:3. Alternate translation: [So he went]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [according to what the man of God had said]

Here the author is speaking of Naaman’s **flesh** as if it were a living thing that could have **returned** to him on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And his flesh became once again like the flesh of a little boy]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a young little boy** has healthy skin, so Naaman did as well. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his skin became healthy again, just like the skin of a little boy]

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in his presence]

If it would appear in your language that Naaman was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [the only true God in all of the earth is in Israel]
See how you translated this expression in 3:23 and 5:6.

Naaman is speaking of himself in the third person as **your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person, here and in the similar instances in verses 17 and 18. Alternate translation: [from me, your servant]

16.note: Following the custom of his culture, Elisha is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred and by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh, to whose face I stand, that I will not take]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in whose presence I stand] or [whose servant I am]

17.note: Naaman is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from earlier in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [But if you will not take a blessing] or [But if you will not accept a gift]

17.q: יֻתַּן־נָ֣א לְ⁠עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֔ מַשָּׂ֥א צֶֽמֶד־פְּרָדִ֖ים אֲדָמָ֑ה כִּ֡י לֽוֹא־יַעֲשֶׂה֩ ע֨וֹד עַבְדְּ⁠ךָ֜ עֹלָ֤ה וָ⁠זֶ֨בַח֙ לֵ⁠אלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֔ים כִּ֖י אִם־לַ⁠יהוָֽה
17.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since your servant will no longer make a burnt offering or sacrifice to other gods, but rather to Yahweh, let dirt, the burden of a pair of mules, please be given to your servant]

The expression **let dirt, the burden of a pair of mules, please be given** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [please give dirt, the burden of a pair of mules, to your servant]

Naaman’s request to **be given** a **load** of **earth** was a symbolic action by which he showed that he wanted to worship only Yahweh, not any of the gods of his home country of Aram. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [let dirt, the burden of a pair of mules, please be given to your servant so that I can build an altar to Yahweh on soil from Israel]

18.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters often speak of a temple as a “house.” Alternate translation: [to the temple of Rimmon]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peacefully]

20.q: חַי־יְהוָה֙ כִּֽי־אִם־רַ֣צְתִּי אַחֲרָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠לָקַחְתִּ֥י מֵ⁠אִתּ֖⁠וֹ מְאֽוּמָה
20.note: Following the custom of his culture, Gehazi is swearing an oath by something that he holds sacred and by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh that I am going to run after him and take something from him]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author or a character may use the word “hand,” part of a person, to represent the whole person in the act of doing something. In this instance, Gehazi is using the **hand** of Naaman to represent him in the act of having gifts that he wanted to offer to Elisha. Alternate translation: [from him]

21.note: Naaman is using the term **Peace** as a common greeting of this culture. He is using it in a question form in order to ask Gehazi if everything is all right. In the next verse, Gehazi uses it in a statement form to reply that everything is all right. (The usage here is different from the one in 4:23 and 4:26, where the Shunammite woman used the word to indicate that she did not want someone to ask any further questions.) Alternate translation: [Is all well]

22.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In this case, it is a quotation not of what Elisha said to Gehazi but of what Gehazi claims Elisha wanted him to say to Naaman. Alternate translation: [and he told me to tell you]

22.q: לֵ⁠אמֹר֒ הִנֵּ֣ה עַתָּ֡ה זֶ֠ה בָּ֣אוּ אֵלַ֧⁠י שְׁנֵֽי־נְעָרִ֛ים מֵ⁠הַ֥ר אֶפְרַ֖יִם מִ⁠בְּנֵ֣י הַ⁠נְּבִיאִ֑ים תְּנָ⁠ה־נָּ֤א לָ⁠הֶם֙ כִּכַּר־כֶּ֔סֶף וּ⁠שְׁתֵּ֖י חֲלִפ֥וֹת בְּגָדִֽים
22.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [asking me to tell you that two young men from the sons of the prophets had just come to him from the hill country of Ephraim and to ask you to give them a kikkar of silver and two changes of clothing]
See how you decided to represent the value of a kikkar in 5:5.

23.q: וַ⁠יָּצַר֩ כִּכְּרַ֨יִם כֶּ֜סֶף בִּ⁠שְׁנֵ֣י חֲרִטִ֗ים וּ⁠שְׁתֵּי֙ חֲלִפ֣וֹת בְּגָדִ֔ים
23.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **two changes of clothes** with the information about the **two silver kikkars**. Alternate translation: [and he bound two silver kikkars and two changes of clothes in two bags]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:12. Alternate translation: [in front of him]

24.note: The author assumes that readers will know what **hill** he means, so he does not specify which hill this was among the many in Samaria. The idea seems to be that Gehazi believed that if he went any farther, Elisha would be able to see him and Naaman’s servants from his house. So this seems to have been a hill that blocked the view from Elisha’s house. If that is the case, then the term **house** refers to Gehazi’s personal quarters rather than to the house in which Elisha lived. Alternate translation: [to a hill that blocked Elisha’s view … in his own quarters]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:20. Alternate translation: [from them]

25.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he came** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between what Naaman’s servants did, as described in the previous verse (leave without being seen), and what Gehazi did (appear before Elisha). Alternate translation: [But he came openly]

Elisha is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [From where have you come]

Gehazi is speaking of himself in the third person as **Your servant** to show humility. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a humble form in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, your servant,]

Gehazi is using **here or there** as a common expression of his culture to mean “anywhere.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [anywhere]

26.q: לֹא־לִבִּ֣⁠י הָלַ֔ךְ כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֧ר הָֽפַךְ־אִ֛ישׁ מֵ⁠עַ֥ל מֶרְכַּבְתּ֖⁠וֹ לִ⁠קְרָאתֶ֑⁠ךָ הַ⁠עֵ֞ת לָ⁠קַ֤חַת אֶת־הַ⁠כֶּ֨סֶף֙ וְ⁠לָ⁠קַ֣חַת בְּגָדִ֔ים וְ⁠זֵיתִ֤ים וּ⁠כְרָמִים֙ וְ⁠צֹ֣אן וּ⁠בָקָ֔ר וַ⁠עֲבָדִ֖ים וּ⁠שְׁפָחֽוֹת
26.note: Elisha is using the question form for emphasis and to rebuke Gehazi. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [My heart went with you when the man turned from upon his chariot to meet you! This is not a time to take silver or to take clothing or olives trees or vineyards or sheep or cattle or male servants or female servants!]

Elisha is speaking as if his **heart** had literally traveled to the place where Gehazi met Naaman. He is using his heart to represent his spirit, and he means that he was aware in his spirit of what Gehazi had done. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Was I not with you in spirit]

26.q: וְ⁠זֵיתִ֤ים וּ⁠כְרָמִים֙ וְ⁠צֹ֣אן וּ⁠בָקָ֔ר וַ⁠עֲבָדִ֖ים וּ⁠שְׁפָחֽוֹת
26.note: The implication is that Gehazi wanted to use the silver he took from Naaman to buy these things. You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to buy olives trees or vineyards or sheep or cattle or male servants or female servants]

27.note: Elisha is speaking of **the leprosy of Naaman** as if it were a living thing that could **cling** to Gehazi and his descendants. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now the leprosy of Naaman will afflict you and your seed]

Elisha is speaking as if the descendants of Gehazi were actually **seed**, the way plants produce seed from which other plants grow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to your descendants]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [from his presence]

The word **afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [leprous like snow]

The point of this comparison is that just as **snow** is white, so Gehazi’s skin became white from the leprosy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as white as snow with leprosy]
